tldr: To assess the ability of video generation models to transform abundant egocentric human manipulation videos into robot manipulation videos, the authors introduce a new benchmark called H2R-Bench. It evaluates models across five dimensions: task goals, action events, functional contacts, embodiment correctness, and video quality. Evaluating 11 state-of-the-art video generation models revealed that even when videos look visually stunning, models often fail to correctly replace human hands with specified robotic end-effectors or maintain functional contact relationships.
hero_caption: A comparison between existing video benchmarks and H2R-Bench. Standard benchmarks (Quality Bench) only evaluate visual smoothness and physical plausibility, giving high scores equally to videos where human hands remain (Model A) and videos transformed to robots (Model B). In contrast, H2R-Bench rigorously diagnoses whether the specified robot embodiment is correctly substituted and whether functional contact with objects is preserved.
overview:
Scaling robot learning requires vast amounts of demonstration data, but collecting real-world robot manipulation data is extremely expensive and time-consuming. On the other hand, egocentric (first-person) videos of humans performing everyday tasks with head-mounted cameras are abundant on the web. Recently, using video generation AI and world models to convert human demonstration videos into videos of robots performing the same tasks has attracted significant attention as a promising data source for robot learning.

However, there has been no diagnostic framework to evaluate whether these generated videos are actually usable as robot data. Conventional video evaluation benchmarks focus primarily on visual appeal or text alignment. They cannot measure cross-embodiment transfer accuracy—such as whether human hands are correctly replaced with robotic arms or grippers, and whether object contacts and task goals are preserved.

To bridge this gap, the authors built H2R-Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate the capability to transform human demonstration videos into manipulation videos of specified robots (parallel-jaw grippers or dexterous hands). Spanning six manipulation families from rigid body manipulation to deformable objects and granular materials, the benchmark contains 120 video clips (totaling 240 transfer cases). Using state-of-the-art multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) as evaluators, it scores generated videos from five distinct perspectives: goal-state completion, action-event completion, functional contact transfer, embodiment correctness, and general video quality.

Evaluating 11 state-of-the-art commercial and open-source video generation models revealed a striking fact. There is virtually no correlation ($\rho=0.14$) between general video quality scores (visual appeal) and overall transfer success (H2RCore). Many visually stunning videos still displayed human hands or generated end-effectors different from the prompt, demonstrating that current world models face substantial hurdles in cross-embodiment transfer.
contributions: Proposed H2R-Bench, a novel source-relative benchmark to evaluate video transformation from egocentric human demonstrations into specified robot embodiments.

Constructed 240 evaluation cases spanning six physical state-change categories and two robot embodiments (parallel-jaw gripper and dexterous hand), complete with structured annotations for goals, actions, contacts, and embodiments.

Developed a five-dimension transfer evaluation protocol covering goal-state completion, action events, functional contact, embodiment correctness, and video quality, achieving an automated evaluation framework with high human agreement ($\rho=0.883$).
Extensively benchmarked 11 leading commercial and open-source models, demonstrating a stark divergence between visual appeal and robot manipulation transfer accuracy.

sections.heading: Looks Aren't Everything: Why We Need a Dedicated Benchmark for Human-to-Robot Video Transfer
sections.summary: To address the high cost of collecting robot data, converting abundant egocentric human videos into robot videos using generative models has drawn great interest. However, existing metrics only evaluate visual beauty and fail to diagnose whether robot morphology and object contacts are correctly reproduced. This paper introduces H2R-Bench to rigorously assess the preservation of task intent and contact relationships across five dimensions.
sections.details:
The biggest bottleneck in scaling robot learning is data collection. Teleoperating physical robots demands extensive hardware setup, calibration, and safety precautions. In contrast, first-person human videos abound in everyday life, naturally capturing object affordances and contact interactions. To bridge this gap, recent research explores using video world models as a bridge from humans to robots, synthesizing robot execution videos directly from human demonstrations.

The core challenge here is not merely hallucinating a plausible robot video. The model must preserve the task intent and object interactions shown in the original human video while adapting them to a completely different physical embodiment.

However, existing video generation benchmarks (see Table 1) mostly measure general visual quality, such as resolution, temporal consistency, and text alignment. Even recent robotics benchmarks focus solely on synthesizing robot videos from text prompts or initial static images; they cannot diagnose whether cross-embodiment transfer—taking a human video as input and replacing the agent with a designated robot—succeeds.

H2R-Bench was created to solve this problem. Covering six manipulation families—rigid body translation, articulated mechanisms, insertion and assembly, deformable object manipulation, granular and bulk materials, and surface/material modification—it rigorously assesses across five dimensions (M1 to M5) whether models correctly replace human hands with target end-effectors while preserving functional contact.

captions.F1: Comparison between existing evaluations and H2R-Bench. Standard quality benchmarks assign high scores even to failed videos where human hands remain intact (Model A). In contrast, H2R-Bench accurately detects whether the specified embodiment was substituted and whether contact succeeded.

sections.heading: Video World Models and Cross-Domain Transfer Between Humans and Robots
sections.summary: Video generation models are evolving into world models that predict physical dynamics, showing great promise for robotics. While transferring knowledge from human videos to robots is actively researched, there has been no comprehensive benchmark to assess whether generated videos faithfully transfer the original manipulation tasks and contacts.
sections.details:
This work builds on three primary research trends:

- Video Generation and World Models for Robotics
Recently, video generative AI has dramatically improved temporal consistency and physical simulation capabilities, emerging as world models that predict object state changes and interaction outcomes. They are increasingly expected to predict future robot observations and supplement scarce real-world data.

- Human-to-Robot Video Transfer (H2R Transfer)
To train robot policies from first-person human demonstrations, researchers have explored visual representation learning, affordance extraction, and image-editing or generative models that repaint human hands into robot arms. However, objective criteria to evaluate how faithfully these generative models transfer operational evidence from source videos have been lacking.

- Current Benchmarks and Their Limitations
General video benchmarks like VBench, as well as recent robotics world model evaluations, typically evaluate generation conditioned on text instructions or initial frames. H2R-Bench differs decisively by evaluating whether a model conditioned on a specific human demonstration video can faithfully reproduce its task intent and contacts under a designated robot embodiment.

captions.F2: The overall pipeline of H2R-Bench. In the top row, egocentric human videos and prompts are provided as input, and each generative model synthesizes two robot embodiment videos. The bottom row illustrates the six target task families and example evaluation profiles across models.

sections.heading: Task Design and the Five Evaluation Axes: A Scoring Protocol That Checks Contacts and Embodiments
sections.summary: H2R-Bench selects 120 videos from EgoDex and evaluates them across 240 cases covering both parallel-jaw grippers and dexterous hands. The protocol comprises five metrics: goal-state completion (M1), action-event completion (M2), functional contact transfer (M3), embodiment correctness (M4), and video quality (M5), unified into the H2RCore score to quantify genuine transfer capability.
sections.details:
The benchmark design and evaluation protocol of H2R-Bench are structured as follows:

- Task Formulation
Each evaluation instance consists of a source human video $V_i^h$, a target robot embodiment $e_i$ (parallel-jaw gripper or dexterous hand), and a prompt $p_i$. The model is instructed to reproduce the manipulation with the specified robot while maintaining the original scene, objects, and interactions. The robot does not need to duplicate human joint trajectories exactly; it is considered successful if it achieves the same functional task goal with the target embodiment.

- Benchmark Construction
The authors curated 120 video clips (5 seconds each) with clear object state changes from the EgoDex dataset. Tasks fall into six manipulation families based on physical state changes: rigid body translation (F1), articulated mechanisms (F2), insertion and assembly (F3), deformable object manipulation (F4), granular and bulk material transfer (F5), and surface/material modification (F6). Crossing these with two embodiments yields 240 transfer cases. Each video is accompanied by structured annotations for goal states, action events, and contact regions, drafted by Qwen3.7-Plus and thoroughly verified by humans.

- Native Input Protocol
To evaluate each model fairly under its optimal capabilities, models supporting full video input receive the complete source clip, while image-conditioned models receive temporally sampled frame sequences. Furthermore, to evaluate the ability to substitute embodiments from text guidance alone, no robot reference image is provided in the primary evaluation.

- Five Metrics (M1 to M5) and H2RCore
Generated videos are independently evaluated on a 0-to-4 rubric by three MLLM judges: Gemini 3.5 Flash, Qwen3.7-Plus, and GPT-5.4.
1. M1: Goal-State Completion ($S_{\mathrm{goal}}$) checks whether object placement or state changes are satisfied in the final frame.
2. M2: Action-Event Completion ($S_{\mathrm{action}}$) checks whether key sub-actions (e.g., grasp, insert, pour) were executed.
3. M3: Functional Contact Transfer ($S_{\mathrm{contact}}$) checks whether the robot establishes functionally equivalent contact with the object as seen in the source video.
4. M4: Embodiment Correctness ($S_{\mathrm{emb}}$) verifies that human hands are absent and the specified end-effector (gripper or hand) is maintained throughout. Videos where human hands perform the primary manipulation receive a score of 0.
5. M5: Video Quality ($S_{\mathrm{video}}$) measures standard visual clarity and temporal smoothness using MUSIQ, CLIP aesthetic scores, and inter-frame differences.

The composite metric H2RCore is calculated on a 100-point scale by weighting contact (M3) and embodiment (M4) at 30% each, goal (M1) and action (M2) at 15% each, and video quality (M5) at 10%. This prevents high scores for videos that merely look pretty or succeed while leaving human hands intact.

sections.heading: Benchmarking 11 Models: High Video Quality Does Not Guarantee Successful Robot Transfer
sections.summary: Testing 11 commercial and open-source models showed that video-conditioned models like Seedance 2.0 and Wan2.7 led the rankings. Crucially, the model with the highest visual quality score (M5) scored near the bottom in transfer capability (H2RCore), highlighting the gap between visual fidelity and embodiment transfer. In addition, transferring to dexterous hands proved easier than to parallel-jaw grippers due to structural similarity to human hands.
sections.details:
The experiments evaluated five commercial models (Seedance 2.0, Wan2.7, Kling-V3, Veo 3.1, and Grok Imagine Video) and six open-source models (Wan2.2, LTX-2.3, HunyuanVideo 1.5-I2V, SkyReels-V3-R2V, LongCat, and Mitty-EPIC14B).

- Main Results (Table 2)
Video-conditioned models capable of ingesting the entire source video dominated the top spots. Seedance 2.0 ranked first (gripper: 77.3, dexterous hand: 84.6), followed closely by Wan2.7 (76.5, 83.1) and Kling-V3 (74.5, 81.7). While goal completion (M1) and action completion (M2) were relatively competitive across models, contact (M3) and embodiment correctness (M4) created significant divergence.

- The Gap Between Visual Quality and Transfer Capability
The rank correlation between visual quality (M5) and H2RCore was only $\rho=0.14$. For example, HunyuanVideo 1.5-I2V achieved the highest visual quality M5 among all models (approx. 0.81), but scored nearly zero on embodiment M4 and only around 0.185 on contact M3, resulting in a low H2RCore score. Similarly, Veo 3.1 achieved top-tier goal completion M1 (0.725), yet scored extremely low on embodiment M4 (0.100 to 0.227) because it failed to replace the human hands with robots.

- Impact of Embodiment: Gripper vs. Dexterous Hand
In 9 out of 11 models, dexterous hands scored higher than parallel-jaw grippers (averaging +3.3 points in H2RCore). Because dexterous hands structurally resemble human hands, maintaining contact relationships while swapping the end-effector proved less disruptive.

- Human Evaluation Agreement
Validating the MLLM judges against annotations from three human evaluators across 660 videos revealed a Spearman rank correlation of $\rho=0.883$ and a Pearson correlation of $r=0.930$, confirming the reliability of the automated evaluation framework.

captions.F3: Correlation matrix showing agreement between human evaluators and each MLLM judge (Gemini, Qwen, GPT). For both dexterous hands (a) and parallel-jaw grippers (b), correlation coefficients between humans and MLLMs exceed 0.8, demonstrating the validity of the automated evaluations.
captions.F5: Qualitative examples of scooping ice cubes with a spoon into a cup. Seedance 2.0 successfully completes the task by holding the spoon with a robotic hand, whereas HunyuanVideo 1.5-I2V leaves the human hand intact, and Veo 3.1 generates an end-effector different from the prompt.

sections.heading: Appendix: Breaking Down Failure Modes and the Sharp Drop From Sparse Frame Inputs
sections.summary: The appendix provides an in-depth analysis of failure modes and input frame ablation experiments. Providing a sparse set of 9 subsampled frames instead of the complete video caused transfer scores (H2RCore) to plummet by up to 41.4 points, despite visual quality remaining unchanged.
sections.details:
The appendix reports several insightful findings expanding on the main results:

- Analysis of Diagnostic Failure Rates
Image- and frame-conditioned models frequently suffered from 'human-led manipulation' (where human hands remained) and contact region mismatches. In parallel-jaw grippers, models often generated a robotic arm while rendering the wrong end-effector tool at the tip.

- Input Frame Ablation Experiments
Using Seedance 2.0, the authors compared the default setting (full video input) with a setting that provided 9 evenly sampled frames from the video (Table S3). While goal completion (M1) held up reasonably well with 9 frames, contact (M3) and embodiment (M4) deteriorated sharply. H2RCore dropped by 27.6 points for grippers and 41.4 points for dexterous hands, while visual quality M5 changed by less than 0.02. Without continuous temporal cues across the entire video, models tended to abandon embodiment transfer and simply reproduce the original human demonstrator.

- Effect of Robot Reference Images
When supplying an additional reference image of the target robot (Table 4), results varied by architecture. Models like Wan2.7 significantly improved their embodiment recognition and boosted scores, whereas models like Kling-V3 and Seedance experienced score drops.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Looking Ahead: Toward Video World Models That Bridge Embodiments
sections.summary: H2R-Bench is the first benchmark to comprehensively evaluate cross-embodiment transfer from human manipulation videos to robot videos. Experiments show that even state-of-the-art video generative models still face substantial hurdles in morphology transformation and functional contact preservation. This work provides a foundation for developing world models that turn human video data into reliable training resources for robots.
sections.details:
This study introduced H2R-Bench to diagnose the ability of generative models to transform egocentric human manipulation demonstrations into robot manipulation videos. Benchmarking 11 leading video generation models across six manipulation categories, two robot embodiments, and five evaluation dimensions revealed an undeniable gap between visual synthesis quality and true robotic transfer capabilities.

While current video generation models excel at synthesizing visually natural scenes, they struggle to simultaneously fulfill morphological requirements: operating with the designated robot end-effector, maintaining appropriate functional contact, and successfully completing the task.

The authors anticipate that H2R-Bench will serve as a widely adopted diagnostic tool, helping bridge the embodiment gap between humans and robots and advancing next-generation video world models that convert the vast ocean of human video data into valuable assets for robot learning.

takeaways: Visual quality scores (e.g., VBench) and robot transfer capability show virtually no correlation ($\rho=0.14$), proving that dedicated transfer diagnostics are indispensable for robotics applications.
In current human-to-robot video transfer, video-conditioned models that ingest complete source videos (such as Seedance and Wan2.7) hold a massive advantage over sparse-frame-conditioned models.
Transferring from human hands to dexterous hands is easier than to parallel-jaw grippers in terms of preserving contact and embodiment, owing to morphological similarity.

When leveraging generative video AI for robot data augmentation, practitioners must independently verify that human hands are removed and that functional contacts are correctly established in the generated videos.
limitations: The benchmark evaluates visual transfer evidence within videos, but does not verify whether low-level robot control policies trained on these generated videos can successfully execute on physical hardware (physical executability).
Evaluation is limited to short 5-second clips curated from EgoDex; handling long-horizon, complex sequential manipulation tasks remains future work.
In scenarios with heavy occlusion or subtle, microscopic contacts, automated scoring by multimodal LLMs may retain some judgment uncertainty.
